kurals.tamil:
அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல் கண்டும் எவன்நெஞ்சே
நீஎமக்கு ஆகா தது.
kurals.transliteration:
Avarnenju avarkkaadhal kandum evannenjae
nee-emakku aakaa thadhu.
kurals.meaning: My heart, you have seen how his heart stays loyal to him alone; why, then, will you not stay loyal to me?
kurals.elementary: Imagine two friends on a team. One friend’s helper always sticks by him, but your own helper keeps running over to the other side. You would ask, ‘Why aren’t you on my side?’ The wife in this poem asks her own heart that same question.
kurals.university: The chapter title neñcoṭu pulattal means ‘sulking with (one’s own) heart’: in the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, the husband has returned, the wife wishes to stage a lovers’ quarrel (ūṭal/pulavi) over his long absence, but her heart refuses to cooperate and rushes toward him, so she turns her reproach on the heart itself. Here she observes that avar neñcu avarkku ātal (‘his heart being his own’, i.e. siding with him and not thinking of her) is plain to see, yet her heart (neñcē) will not be emakku (‘ours’, on her side). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read ātal as ‘becoming a companion/ally (tuṇai)’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar add that her heart keeps melting toward him instead; Pope renders it ‘You see his heart is his alone; O heart, why not be all my own?’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the chapter title is printed நெஞ்சொடுபுலத்தல் on ytamizh and நெஞ்சோடு புலத்தல் on thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad pictures the self as the rider in a chariot, the body as the chariot, intelligence as the charioteer and the mind as the reins, with the senses as horses; for one without understanding, the senses run wild like vicious horses that will not obey their driver.
hinduism.explanation: The image shows the mind as something meant to serve the self but able to pull away from it.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s heart behaves like reins slipping from the driver’s hand, running toward the husband instead of obeying her.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known chariot passage; a real image of a mind that will not stay under one’s control, though its concern is spiritual discipline, not a lover’s quarrel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a self divided against itself, wanting one thing while doing another.
christianity.tie_back: The wife meets the same split: she wills to hold back from her husband, yet her heart goes the other way.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on the divided will, though Paul speaks of sin, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: In the story of Yusuf, this confession admits that one’s own soul (nafs) pushes toward what the person knows she should resist.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s speaker, the confessor admits that her own inner self has not been on her side.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a genuine parallel on the self working against one’s own resolve in a story of love, but the verse speaks of moral wrongdoing, not a wife’s pride.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why moanest thou within me? Hope thou in God; for I shall yet praise Him for the salvation of His countenance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist speaks to his own soul as if it were a second person, questioning and rebuking it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same form, a person addressing her own heart and asking why it acts as it does.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a close formal match on speaking to one’s own soul, though the psalm longs for God rather than reproaching love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that one’s own badly aimed mind can hurt a person more than any outside enemy.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife finds that her own heart, not her husband, is the one working against her.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a good match on the mind as one’s own adversary, though the Dhammapada is about moral discipline, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi teaches King Srenika that a person’s own self can be either friend or enemy.
jainism.tie_back: The wife complains that her heart, which ought to be her friend, has gone over to the other side.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a real parallel on the self as friend or foe, though the Jain verse concerns karma and liberation, not love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a short fragment Sappho says that she does not know what to do, because her mind is split in two.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet describes love leaving her inner self divided and unable to settle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels the same split: one part of her wants to sulk while her heart wants to run to him.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 51 (paraphrase; cf. tr. D.A. Campbell, Greek Lyric I)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very short fragment whose context is lost; a fair match on a mind divided by love, though not a quarrel with one’s own heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal holds that the heart moves by a logic of its own that the reasoning mind cannot overrule.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s reason says to hold back; her heart, following its own reasons, goes to him anyway.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line; a strong match on the heart acting apart from reason, though Pascal applies it mainly to faith.

kurals.tamil:
உறாஅ தவர்க்கண்ட கண்ணும் அவரைச்
செறாஅரெனச் சேறியென் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Uraaa thavarkkanda kannum avaraich
cheraa-arenach chaeriyen nenju.
kurals.meaning: My heart, even after seeing that he does not care for me, you still go to him, telling yourself he will not be angry.
kurals.elementary: Think of a puppy that keeps running to someone who ignores it, wagging its tail and hoping for a pat. The puppy does not stop to think. The wife says her heart is like that puppy: it runs to her husband even when he has not shown much love.
kurals.university: Uṟāatavar is ‘one who does not draw near’, i.e. who shows no love (uṟu, to approach, be attached); ceṟāar is ‘he will not be angry’, and cēṟi ‘you go’. Both uṟāa and ceṟāa show the long-vowel extension (aḷapeṭai) used for metre, also seen in 1295. The commentators agree on the sense: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan have the heart go to the beloved ‘thinking he will not hate us’, and Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘thinking he will not be angry if we go’; Pope renders ‘Why go to him as though he were not enemy?’ The point within the chapter is that the heart’s eagerness undercuts the wife’s plan to sulk. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha learns that Krishna is dancing with other cowherd women, yet in her loneliness her heart keeps recalling him and longing for him rather than turning away.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva shows Radha unable to stop loving Krishna even when he seems indifferent to her.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heart, Radha’s heart goes on seeking a beloved who, for now, does not seem to seek her.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canto; a good match on love that keeps going to an inattentive beloved, though Jayadeva’s frame is devotional.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as endlessly patient and willing to hope for the best.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart ‘believes all things’: it hopes he will not be angry even after seeing his coldness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a fair match on love that keeps hoping, though Paul praises this, while the Kural’s speaker scolds it.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that what the heart loves is not always what is good for it.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart loves one who does not love it back, against what she can plainly see.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a loose next-best match on misplaced love, from a verse whose context is fighting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song keeps seeking her beloved even after he has withdrawn and does not answer.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, love goes on reaching toward a beloved who seems to hold himself back.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a strong match on pursuing a beloved who has turned away, though the Song does not reproach the heart for it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful, indeed, it is to subdue the mind, so difficult to subdue, ever swift, and seizing whatever it desires. A tamed mind brings happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the untrained mind as quick to grab at whatever it wants.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart rushes after what it desires without weighing what it has already seen.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a partial match on a mind that runs after its desires, framed as a call to discipline, not as love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that passionate attachment drives a being toward what will hurt it, like a moth to a flame.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart flies toward him just as blindly, though she has seen that he does not care.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a fair image of attraction overriding judgement, but the Jain text condemns attachment, where the Kural only gently scolds it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo falls in love with Narcissus and follows him through the woods even after he coldly rejects her, wasting away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells of a love that keeps pursuing a beloved who gives nothing back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo’s heart, like the wife’s, goes after one who has shown no love, unable to stop itself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth (Roman retelling of Greek material); a strong match on love following one who does not return it, though Narcissus never loved Echo at all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, and can never by itself oppose a passion in directing the will.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, knowing a fact does not by itself stop desire; feeling drives action.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart knows he is cold, yet that knowledge cannot hold it back from going to him.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous section; a reasonable match on knowledge failing to restrain feeling, though Hume writes about action in general, not love.

kurals.tamil:
கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார்இல் என்பதோ நெஞ்சேநீ
பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kettaarkku nattaar-il enpadho nenjaenee
pettaangu avarpin selal.
kurals.meaning: My heart, is it because ‘the ruined have no friends’ that you leave me and follow him wherever you please?
kurals.elementary: There is an old saying that when someone is in trouble, their friends disappear. The wife feels sad and alone, and even her own heart has left her to go after her husband. So she asks her heart, ‘Did you leave me because I am having a hard time?’
kurals.university: The first line quotes a proverb: keṭṭārkku naṭṭār il, ‘the ruined have no friends’; the wife bitterly applies it to herself, worn down by separation. Peṭṭāṅku means ‘as you please, at your own desire’ and avar piṉ celal ‘going after him’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read keṭṭār as ‘those ruined by suffering’, and Kalaignar puts it as ‘those destroyed by sorrow have no friends to stand by them’; Pope renders ‘The ruined have no friends, they say; and so, my heart, / To follow him, at thy desire, from me thou dost depart.’ The rhetorical question (eṉpatō, ‘is it that…?’) carries the chapter’s tone of affectionate reproach. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a boat on the water is swept away by a strong wind, even one of the senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man’s intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that the mind, once fixed on one object, can sweep a person’s judgement away with it.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s heart, fixed on her husband, is carried off after him, leaving her judgement behind.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a good image of the mind being carried off by its object, though the Gita counsels sense-control rather than describing love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the heart follows whatever a person values most.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s treasure is her husband, so her heart goes where he is, whatever she tells it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on the heart following what it treasures, though Jesus speaks of earthly versus heavenly riches.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you seen the one who takes as his god his own desire? Then would you be responsible for him?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a person who simply follows wherever desire leads.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart goes peṭṭāṅku, ‘as it pleases’, following its desire rather than her will.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a loose next-best match on following one’s desire, with a far stronger moral judgement than the Kural’s tender reproach.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song rises and goes out through the city in search of her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: Her soul goes after the one it loves, just as the wife’s heart follows her husband.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a strong match on the soul going after the beloved, though without the Kural’s complaint against the heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dwelling in the cave (of the heart), the mind, without form, wanders far and alone. Those who subdue this mind are liberated from the bonds of Mara.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the mind as roaming far from its owner on its own.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart has wandered far off after her husband and left her behind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a fair match on the mind wandering off alone, though the verse calls for subduing it, not loving.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Prince Neminatha turned back from his own wedding procession and renounced the world, his bride Rajimati was left grief-stricken; yet her heart stayed fixed on him, and in time she too renounced and followed the path he had taken.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition tells of a bride whose love for Nemi led her to follow him even after he left her.
jainism.tie_back: Like the wife’s heart in the Kural, Rajimati’s heart goes after the one who has gone away from her.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known Rajimati–Neminatha story; she follows him into renunciation rather than into married love, so the match is only partial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Clytie, abandoned by the sun god Helios, sits on the bare ground day after day, turning her face to follow his course across the sky until she becomes the heliotrope, the flower that always faces the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells of a rejected lover whose whole being keeps turning after the one who left her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Clytie’s gaze follows Helios just as the wife’s heart follows her husband.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth in Ovid’s Roman retelling; a strong match on love that keeps following, though Clytie is wholly rejected while the Kural’s couple are married.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how humans were once double beings who were split in two, so that each half now longs for and pursues its missing other half.
philosophy.explanation: The myth explains love as the pull of a part toward the whole it belongs to.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart behaves as if it belongs with him, and so it leaves her to go after its other half.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous speech; a reasonable match on love pulling the self toward the beloved, though Aristophanes offers a comic myth, not a lover’s reproach.

kurals.tamil:
இனிஅன்ன நின்னொடு சூழ்வார்யார் நெஞ்சே
துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்காண் மற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Ini-anna ninnodu soozhvaaryaar nenjae
thuniseydhu thuvvaaikaan matru.
kurals.meaning: My heart, you will not first sulk and then enjoy the making-up; so who will ever plan such things with you again?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you and a friend plan to act a little upset with someone to show your feelings, and then make up. But the moment that person walks in, your friend runs and hugs him. You might say, ‘I’m never planning anything with you again!’ That is what the wife says to her heart.
kurals.university: Tuṉi is a strong form of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking), and tuvvāy means ‘you will not enjoy’; the commentators read the line as ‘you will not first sulk and then enjoy (the reunion that follows)’. In Tamil love poetics the reconciliation after ūṭal is itself a pleasure, which is why the wife complains that her eager heart skips it. Iṉi aṉṉa niṉṉoṭu cūḻvār yār, ‘hereafter who will consult with you about such things?’, is her mock threat to stop taking the heart into her counsels; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar add ‘I will not’. Pope renders ‘See, thou first show offended pride, and then submit, I bade; / Henceforth such council who will share with thee my heart?’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, when Krishna comes back to Radha, she at first holds on to her wounded pride (mana), and her friend urges her to give up the sulk and go to him while the moment lasts.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva stages the lovers’ quarrel and its reconciliation as a set stage of love.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha can sustain the sulk that the Kural’s heart cannot; both poems treat quarrel-then-reunion as part of love’s pleasure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a genuine parallel on the convention of the lovers’ sulk, though here the heroine holds out where the Kural’s heart gives in too soon.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows anger but tells believers to let it go quickly.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart lets its anger go even faster than Paul asks, before it has served its purpose.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a loose next-best link on short-lived anger, with none of the Kural’s playful lovers’ quarrel.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hold back anger and forgive.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart forgives at once, but she wishes it had held its displeasure a little longer.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a loose link on quick forgiveness, which the Qur’an praises and the Kural’s speaker playfully regrets.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my heart was moved for him.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song first makes excuses not to open to her beloved, then her heart is stirred and she rises.
judaism.tie_back: Her show of reluctance melts the moment he appears, much as the wife’s heart gives up its sulk at once.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a reasonable match on feigned reluctance overcome by the heart, though not explicitly a lovers’ quarrel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a fletcher straightens an arrow shaft, even so the discerning man straightens his mind — so fickle and unsteady, so difficult to guard.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the mind fickle and hard to keep on a chosen course.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart could not keep to the plan they had made; it wavered the moment he came home.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a next-best match on a fickle mind that will not hold a resolve, with no connection to love’s quarrels.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that it is one’s own love or aversion, not the object, that throws the mind from one state to another.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart swings from planned anger to eager love the moment it sees him, just the kind of change the sutra describes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only a loose next-best link on love overturning a planned mood, in an ascetic text that would reject the Kural’s whole game of love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns, Penelope does not rush to embrace him; though her son calls her heart harder than stone, she holds back and tests him with the secret of their bed before she yields and runs to him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a wife who keeps her composure before the joyful reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope manages the reserve before reunion that the Kural’s wife wanted, and her heart would not allow.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 23.85-240 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a partial match on reserve before reunion, though Penelope’s motive is caution, not a lover’s sulk.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy The Girl from Andros, a character remarks that lovers’ quarrels are the renewal of love (amantium irae amoris integratio est).
philosophy.explanation: The line, which became proverbial, holds that a quarrel between lovers ends by making their love fresh again.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the pleasure the wife says her heart throws away by refusing to quarrel first.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous proverbial line from Roman comedy rather than a philosophical treatise; a close match on quarrel as love’s renewal.

kurals.tamil:
பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின்பிரிவு அஞ்சும்
அறாஅ இடும்பைத்தென் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Peraaamai anjum perinpirivu anjum
araaa idumpaiththen nenju.
kurals.meaning: When he is away my heart fears it will not have him; when he is here it fears he will leave; so my heart is never free of pain.
kurals.elementary: Think of a child waiting for a favourite toy: before getting it, she worries she never will, and after getting it, she worries she will lose it. The wife’s heart is like that with her husband: worried when he is gone, and worried when he is home that he will go again.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on parallel clauses: peṟāamai añcum (‘it fears not having him’) and peṟiṉ pirivu añcum (‘having him, it fears separation’), leading to aṟāa iṭumpaittu eṉ neñcu, ‘my heart is (a thing) of unceasing distress’. Peṟāamai and aṟāa again show metrical vowel lengthening (aḷapeṭai). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan agree on the reading; Solomon Pappaiah makes the setting explicit, ‘when my husband was away… when he has come’. Pope renders ‘I fear I shall not gain, I fear to lose him when I gain; / And thus my heart endures unceasing pain.’ Within the chapter this explains why the heart cannot afford to sulk: even in his presence it already fears his next departure. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari observes that every worldly good comes with its own fear: in enjoyment there is fear of disease, in family pride fear of a fall, in wealth fear of kings, and so on, so that only detachment is free of fear.
hinduism.explanation: The verse lists how each thing we hold brings the dread of losing it.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s heart lives this exactly: having her husband brings only the fear of losing him.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka, verse beginning bhoge roga-bhayam (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse whose number varies by edition; a good match on possession breeding fear of loss, though Bhartrihari’s answer is renunciation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that perfect love leaves no room for fear, because fear itself is a torment.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart is the opposite case: its love is full of fear, and so it lives in torment.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a contrasting parallel that names fear as love’s torment, though John speaks of love for God.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches calm both over what one lacks and over what one has.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart has neither calm: it frets over what it lacks and over what it might lose.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a structural match on anxiety over lacking and having, offered as a remedy rather than as love poetry.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that waiting for what one longs for wears the heart down.
judaism.tie_back: The first half of the Kural, the heart afraid while he is away, is this heartsickness; the Kural adds that even fulfilment brings fear.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); matches the first half well, but Proverbs calls fulfilment life-giving where the Kural finds new fear in it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful. Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that loving someone brings pain both in absence and in the threat of separation.
buddhism.tie_back: This names both halves of the wife’s distress: pain at not seeing him and dread of parting from him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match on the pain of absence and of separation, though the Buddha concludes one should hold nothing dear, which the Kural does not.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that attachment brings unhappiness at every stage, in getting, keeping and losing.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart suffers at every stage of her love, whether he is absent or present.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on distress in both lacking and having, though the Jain text aims at giving up attachment altogether.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the loosener of limbs, a bittersweet creature against whom there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho coined the idea of love as sweet and bitter at the same time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The wife’s love is bittersweet in just this way: even its sweetness carries pain.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 130 (paraphrase; cf. tr. D.A. Campbell, Greek Lyric I)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a short fragment; a partial match on love’s mixed sweetness and pain, without the Kural’s two-sided fear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines hope and fear as unsteady pleasure and pain arising from an uncertain outcome, and adds that there is no hope unmingled with fear, and no fear unmingled with hope.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, hope and fear always come together because both rest on uncertainty.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart never escapes fear because its joy in her husband is always shadowed by uncertainty about losing him.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Emotions XII-XIII (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Spinoza’s definitions and explanation; a strong match on hope and fear being inseparable, stated as general psychology, not about love.

kurals.tamil:
தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால் என்னைத்
தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaniye irundhu ninaiththakkaal ennaith
thiniya irundhadhen nenju.
kurals.meaning: Whenever I sat alone and thought of him, my own heart seemed ready to eat me alive.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been alone and kept thinking about something sad until you felt worse and worse? Your thoughts can feel like they are gnawing at you. The wife says that when she was alone, her own heart chewed at her like that.
kurals.university: Taṉiyē iruntu niṉaittakkāl means ‘when I sat alone and thought’, and tiṉiya iruntatu ‘it was there to eat (me)’: the heart, instead of comforting her, devoured her. Commentators differ on what she was thinking of: Mu. Varadarasanar says ‘his faults’ (avaruṭaiya tavaṟukaḷ), which fits the chapter’s quarrel; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar say ‘the separation from her lover’; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the heart, ‘not being a companion to me’, tormented her. Pope renders ‘My heart consumes me when I ponder lone, / And all my lover’s cruelty bemoan.’ The past tense (iruntatu) recalls the time of separation now that he is back. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For the mind is restless, turbulent, obstinate and very strong, O Krsna, and to subdue it is, it seems to me, more difficult than controlling the wind.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna admits that his mind is turbulent and nearly impossible to calm.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife finds her own heart just as turbulent, turning against her when she is alone.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.34 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a fair match on a mind that agitates its owner, though Arjuna speaks of meditation, not grief in love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch.”
christianity.explanation: In Gethsemane Jesus speaks of a sorrow so heavy it seems to crush him.
christianity.tie_back: The wife too feels an inner sorrow strong enough to consume her when she is alone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a loose next-best link on crushing inner sorrow, in a very different, sacred context.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Yaqub, grieving alone for his lost son Yusuf, keeps his sorrow to himself and to God.
islam.tie_back: Like Yaqub, the wife carries a grief that works on her in solitude, though she has only her own heart to speak to.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a partial match on solitary grief for an absent loved one, but Yaqub turns to God, not to his own heart.

judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song says that even when she lies down, her heart stays awake, listening for her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: Like the wife alone at night, her body rests but her heart will not let her be.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a fair match on a restless heart in solitude, though the Song’s tone is expectant rather than tormented.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares painful feeling to being struck by an arrow; the untaught person, by brooding and lamenting over it, is struck by a second arrow of mental pain, while the wise person feels the first and not the second.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows how the mind adds its own suffering on top of what has happened.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s solitary brooding is that second arrow: her own heart adds to the pain of separation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; a good match on the mind tormenting itself, though the sutta’s aim is equanimity, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: Asked how he manages the wild horse that runs about, Gautama tells Kesi that the horse is the mind, unruly and dreadful, and that he keeps it in check by the discipline of the Law.
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue between Kesi and Gautama, the untrained mind is a wild horse that runs where it will.
jainism.tie_back: Left alone, the wife’s heart runs wild like that horse and turns on its rider.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 23 (Kesi and Gautama) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known dialogue, not verified verse by verse this session; only a loose match on an unruly mind, with no reference to grief or love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ariadne, waking alone on the shore of Naxos after Theseus has sailed away, wanders the empty beach recalling him and is consumed by grief and memory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Ariadne shows a woman tormented by her own thoughts once she is left by herself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Ariadne, the wife alone finds her own memories devouring her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known poem; a good match on solitary grief for an absent lover, though Ariadne has been abandoned for good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius begins the Consolation of Philosophy alone in prison, writing laments with the Muses of poetry, who only feed his grief until Lady Philosophy drives them away.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius shows how a mind left to itself in sorrow can nourish its own pain.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart, like Boethius’s Muses, fed her grief when she sat alone.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I, prose 1 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous opening scene; a partial match on solitary brooding that deepens pain, in a context of misfortune rather than love.

kurals.tamil:
நாணும் மறந்தேன் அவர்மறக் கல்லாஎன்
மாணா மடநெஞ்சிற் பட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanum marandhaen avarmarak kallaaen
maanaa madanenjir pattu.
kurals.meaning: Caught up with my foolish, unworthy heart that cannot forget him, I have forgotten even my modesty.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when we miss someone very much, we do things we would normally feel shy about, like crying in front of others or running to hug them in public. The wife says her heart missed her husband so much that she forgot to be shy.
kurals.university: Nāṇ is the feminine modesty or sense of shame that classical Tamil poetics treats as a woman’s guarding virtue; avar maṟakkallā is ‘unable to forget him’, and māṇā maṭa neñcu ‘my undignified, foolish heart’ (māṇā, lacking excellence; maṭam, simplicity/folly). Paṭṭu, ‘having fallen in with’, makes the heart the bad company that led her astray. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan add that nāṇ is ‘something that should not be forgotten’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads the heart as ‘unsteady’ and the husband as one ‘who has forgotten me’. Pope renders ‘Fall’n ’neath the sway of this ignoble foolish heart, / Which will not him forget, I have forgotten shame.’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the cowherd women of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute on the autumn night, they leave their work and families and rush to him in the forest, setting aside the propriety expected of them.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana shows love for Krishna so strong that the gopis forget ordinary restraint.
hinduism.tie_back: As with the gopis, the wife’s longing has overridden the modesty she would normally keep.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous chapter; a strong match on love overriding social modesty, though the gopis’ love is read devotionally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.”
christianity.explanation: A woman at a Pharisee’s dinner, ignoring what the guests think, pours out her love at Jesus’ feet.
christianity.tie_back: Like the wife, she is carried past ordinary decorum by the depth of her feeling.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a partial match on love setting aside social shame, but the love here is penitent devotion, not marital longing.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that faith has many branches and that haya, modesty or a sense of shame, is one branch of faith.
islam.explanation: Islam treats modesty as part of faith itself, not merely good manners.
islam.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same high value for modesty, which is why the wife is dismayed to have lost it.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; it shares the value placed on modesty but offers no parallel to love making one forget it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song wishes she could show her love openly without being scorned.
judaism.tie_back: Both poems feel the tension between love’s urge to show itself and the modesty society expects.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a reasonable match on love straining against public modesty, though the Song’s speaker still holds back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that two bright qualities protect the world, a sense of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa); without them, people would not respect even the bonds of family.
buddhism.explanation: Shame and conscience are treated as the guardians that keep people within bounds.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife laments that love has made her lose nāṇ, a guardian Buddhism also prizes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a short sutta; it shares the high value placed on shame but has nothing about love overpowering it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells monks not even to keep the memory of attraction in their minds.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart does the opposite, unable to stop remembering the beloved, and so loses its restraint.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting parallel on the power of memory over restraint, from a monastic rule that rejects the Kural’s marital love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea, falling in love with Jason, struggles through a sleepless night between shame (aidos) before her father and her passion; in the end love overcomes her shame and she goes to help him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows a young woman whose modesty gives way before love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Medea, the wife finds that her heart’s love has overpowered her sense of shame.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a strong match on love defeating shame, though Medea’s choice betrays her family while the Kural’s wife loves her own husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates pictures the soul as a charioteer with two horses; when the beloved comes into view, the unruly horse, deaf to shame, drags the charioteer and the modest horse toward the beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows passion pulling the soul past its own sense of shame.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart is the unruly horse that has dragged her past her modesty.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a strong match on passion overriding shame, though Plato urges the charioteer to master the horse.

kurals.tamil:
எள்ளின் இளிவாம்என்று எண்ணி அவர்திறம்
உள்ளும் உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellin ilivaam-endru enni avarthiram
ullum uyirkkaadhal nenju.
kurals.meaning: My heart, which loves him as its life, thinks that scorning him would only disgrace itself, and so it dwells on his good qualities instead.
kurals.elementary: When someone you love lets you down, you might want to say mean things about them. But a loving heart thinks, ‘If I say bad things about him, it makes me look bad too,’ and remembers his good side instead. The wife’s heart does exactly that.
kurals.university: Eḷḷiṉ iḷivām means ‘if (I) scorn (him), it will be a disgrace (to me)’; avar tiṟam uḷḷum, ‘it thinks of his qualities (or ways)’. Uyirkkātal neñcu is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as ‘the heart that loves life’ (fearing disgrace as worse than death), while Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar take it as ‘the heart that loves him as its own life’. Commentators also differ on avar tiṟam: ‘his noble qualities’ (Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Kalaignar) versus ‘his coming and our union’ (Pappaiah). Pope renders ‘If I contemn him, then disgrace awaits me evermore; / My soul that seeks to live his virtues numbers o’er.’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana’s grove in Lanka, Sita refuses every attempt to turn her against Rama and keeps her mind on his virtues, declaring that she belongs to him as light belongs to the sun.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana shows Sita’s devotion holding firm and dwelling on Rama’s goodness even in long separation.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Sita, the wife’s heart will not think ill of her absent husband but keeps recalling his good qualities.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known section; a good match on refusing to think ill of an absent husband, though Sita’s setting is captivity, not a lovers’ quarrel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as refusing to think the worst of the beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart ‘thinketh no evil’ of her husband and turns to his good qualities instead.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on love declining to think ill, though Paul’s motive is charity, not avoiding self-disgrace.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells believers to avoid thinking the worst of others.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart refuses to think ill of her husband and chooses to dwell on his merits.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a reasonable match on avoiding negative thoughts about others, given as a general social rule.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The sage teaches that one should always give others the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.tie_back: The wife’s heart judges her husband favourably, dwelling on his good qualities rather than his neglect.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sefaria.org (Kulp translation); a strong match on judging another favourably, framed as general ethics rather than love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada advises not to look for the faults of others or at what they have done or left undone, but only at what one has done or left undone oneself.
buddhism.explanation: The verse turns attention away from another’s failings.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart refuses to dwell on her husband’s faults, though for love rather than self-examination.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse; a partial match on not fixing on another’s faults, with a different, self-searching purpose.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists four attitudes to cultivate: friendliness toward all beings, delight (pramoda) in those with greater virtues, compassion for the afflicted, and equanimity toward the ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics trains the mind to rejoice in others’ good qualities rather than dwell on their faults.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart does something like pramoda, fixing on her husband’s good qualities instead of scorning him.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (Digambara numbering; 7.6 in Svetambara) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutra, not verified word for word this session; only a partial match, since Jain pramoda is a spiritual discipline, not marital love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Alcyone, while her husband Ceyx is away at sea, prays daily to Juno for his safe return and thinks only of his welfare, never of blame.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid portrays a wife whose thoughts of her absent husband are wholly loving.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Alcyone, the wife’s heart dwells on her husband with love rather than complaint.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a partial match on loving thoughts of an absent husband, but Alcyone has no grievance to set aside.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that when someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, you should remember that he acted as he thought right, and so you will be gentle with him.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic refuses to let another’s fault provoke him into contempt.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart, too, declines to answer neglect with scorn.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a partial match on not meeting ill-treatment with contempt, reached by Stoic reasoning rather than love.

kurals.tamil:
துன்பத்திற்கு யாரே துணையாவார் தாமுடைய
நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunpaththirku yaarae thunaiyaavaar thaamudaiya
nenjan thunaiyal vazhi.
kurals.meaning: When one is in trouble, who else will stand by one, if one’s own heart will not?
kurals.elementary: When you feel sad, the first one who can comfort you is you: you can tell yourself, ‘It will be okay.’ But if even your own feelings turn against you, who else can help? The wife asks this when her heart will not stand by her.
kurals.university: Tuṉpattiṟku yārē tuṇaiyāvār, ‘who indeed will be a companion in sorrow?’, with the emphatic -ē, and tām uṭaiya neñcam tuṇai al vaḻi, ‘when the heart that one owns is not a companion’. Here the wife generalises her complaint into a maxim (the plural tām gives it the force of ‘anyone’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress tām urimaiyākap peṟṟa, ‘that one possesses by right’; Kalaignar reads tuṇai as ‘support to bear’ the sorrow. Pope renders ‘And who will aid me in my hour of grief, / If my own heart comes not to my relief?’ With 1300 this forms the chapter’s closing pair of general sayings. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (thirukkural.net prints நெஞ்சந் with the same sandhi).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man must elevate himself by his own mind, not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person’s own mind is meant to be the helper that lifts him up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same: one’s own heart should be the first companion in trouble.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a strong match on one’s own mind as one’s helper, though the Gita’s goal is spiritual uplift.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a person’s own spirit carries him through suffering, but nothing can help when that spirit itself is broken.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point almost exactly: if one’s own heart fails, who else can bear the sorrow?
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a near one-to-one match on one’s own spirit as the support in trouble.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that a heart at peace is the source of steadiness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shares the sense that the heart must be settled to sustain a person, though it sees no other source of help if the heart fails.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a partial match on the heart as the seat of steadiness, but the Qur’an locates its peace in God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self [only], what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that a person must first be his own support before he can look to others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question: if one’s own heart will not stand by one, who will?
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:14 (tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sefaria.org (Kulp translation); a near one-to-one match on self-support, though Hillel adds a turn toward others the Kural lacks.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One truly is the protector of oneself; who else could the protector be? With oneself fully controlled, one gains a mastery that is hard to gain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that no one else can be one’s refuge if one is not one’s own.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same ‘who else?’ question about one’s own heart as one’s companion.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a near one-to-one match on self as one’s only true protector, applied to discipline rather than love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus I became the protector of myself and of others besides, of all living beings, whether they move or not.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi tells how father, mother, brothers, sisters and loving wife all failed to relieve his pain, so that he learned to become his own protector.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, when trouble comes, no outside companion can take the place of one’s own self.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.35, with 20.23-30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good match on the self as one’s only real help in suffering, though Anathi’s answer is renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Lying awake in his own palace among the suitors, Odysseus strikes his breast and speaks to his heart, telling it to endure, since it had endured worse on the day the Cyclops devoured his companions.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a hero turning to his own heart as companion and support in a hard hour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s heart stands by him as the Kural says one’s heart should; the wife’s, sadly, does not.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 20.17-21 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a strong match on the heart as one’s companion in trouble, though Odysseus’s heart obeys him where the wife’s does not.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the good person is of one mind with himself and is his own best friend, while the bad are at variance with themselves and cannot even be friends to themselves.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, being a friend to oneself is the root of every other friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s plight is the divided self Aristotle describes: her own heart is not her friend.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.4 and IX.8 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known chapters; a strong match on self-friendship as the first support, though Aristotle ties it to virtue, not love.

kurals.tamil:
தஞ்சம் தமரல்லர் ஏதிலார் தாமுடைய
நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Thanjam thamarallar aedhilaar thaamudaiya
nenjam thamaral vazhi.
kurals.meaning: When one’s own heart does not act like kin, it is no wonder that strangers do not either.
kurals.elementary: If even your own feelings won’t be kind to you, you can’t be surprised when people you hardly know aren’t kind either. The wife says that since her heart has left her, she can hardly blame others for not standing by her.
kurals.university: Tañcam here is glossed by the commentators as ‘easy, a slight matter’ (eḷitu): Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read ‘it is easy (natural) for strangers (ētilār) not to be kin (tamar allar) when one’s own heart (tām uṭaiya neñcam) is not kin’. Puliyur Kesikan agrees, calling it ‘natural’ (iyalpāṉatē). Sivayogi Sivakumar instead takes tañcam in its other sense, ‘refuge’: ‘there is no kin to give refuge if one’s own heart is not one’s own’, a variant reading of the same text. Pope renders ‘A trifle is unfriendliness by aliens shown, / When our own heart itself is not our own!’ The couplet closes the chapter by turning the wife’s quarrel into a general truth about the self; it is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his very mind will be the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s own mind can be the closest friend or the worst enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: when one’s own heart is not kin, it is a greater blow than any stranger’s coldness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.6 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a strong match on one’s own mind as the closest friend or enemy, though the Gita speaks of yogic self-mastery.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a person divided within cannot stand firm in anything.
christianity.tie_back: The wife, at odds with her own heart, finds she can expect little steadiness from anyone else.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a partial match on inner division, without the Kural’s comparison between one’s heart and strangers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart and that to Him you will be gathered.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that a person does not fully command even his own heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker has found exactly this: her heart is not wholly her own.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a real match on the heart not being fully one’s own, though the verse speaks of God’s power, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The heart knoweth its own bitterness; and with its joy no stranger can intermeddle.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that each heart lives its own inner life that outsiders cannot share.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural draws on the same contrast between one’s own heart and strangers.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a reasonable match on the heart versus the stranger, though Proverbs does not imagine the heart deserting its owner.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither mother, father, nor any other relative can do one greater good than one’s own well-directed mind.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks one’s own well-directed mind above any kinsman as a source of good.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural makes the same comparison: one’s heart should be closer kin than any relative or stranger.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match on one’s own mind as truer kin than relatives, though stated positively rather than as a complaint.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that no outside enemy harms a person as much as his own misdirected self.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural likewise finds one’s own heart a worse betrayer than any stranger.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good match on one’s own self as worse than an outside enemy, though the context is a lapsed monk.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Euripides’ Medea, before her terrible act, says that she understands the evil she is about to do, but her passion (thumos) is stronger than her reasoning.
greek_mythology.explanation: Medea’s own heart overrules her and becomes her worst enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, when one’s own heart is not on one’s side, nothing outside can make up for it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of famous lines; a partial match on a heart that turns against its owner, in a far darker situation than the Kural’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine marvels that the mind commands the body and is obeyed at once, but when the mind commands itself it is resisted.
philosophy.explanation: Augustine finds the strangest disobedience not in others but within his own will.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife discovers the same: the one who will not obey her is her own heart, so strangers’ coldness is no surprise.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a strong match on the self refusing its own command, though Augustine’s struggle is with conversion, not love.
